IBM Heron experiments detected memory signal and generated bytes autoregressively from measured probabilities, but the models showed no claimed quantum advantage and remained worse than classical n-grams.
papers.selection_reason: Explores quantum-native language models with dissipative memory, contributing to the 'Large Language Models' topic.
papers.title: Trainable Quantum-Native Language Models: Dissipative Memory, Capacity Limits, and Hardware Validation
papers.tldr: Trainable dissipative quantum language models can retain information beyond one token and operate on IBM hardware, but remain short-memory, classically simulable, and inferior to classical n-gram baselines.

papers.abstract: Audio-visual speech enhancement (AVSE) improves speech intelligibility in noisy environments but often relies on computationally expensive models unsuitable for resource-constrained edge devices. This paper introduces a reinforcement learning-driven neural architecture search (RL-NAS) framework to discover compact, efficient AVSE architectures. The search space preserves temporal alignment between audio and visual streams, while a novel reward function jointly optimises speech enhancement performance, measured by SI-SNR improvement, and model compactness. Using proximal policy optimisation with constraint-aware action masking, the framework evaluates only 35 candidate architectures and identifies a model with 2.9 million parameters, compared with 22 million in the baseline. The proposed architecture achieves a 14.5 dB SI-SNR improvement, only 0.7 dB below the baseline, while reducing model size by approximately nine-fold. Evaluation on commercial mobile CPUs demonstrates a 4.3-fold reduction in real-time factor, supporting practical on-device deployment. Compared with random search, RL-NAS achieves 92% higher search efficiency. Architectural analysis reveals that shallower but wider temporal convolutional blocks and aggressive visual pathway pruning can maintain enhancement performance while substantially reducing computational requirements. These findings demonstrate the potential of reinforcement learning-guided architecture search for developing lightweight, efficient and deployable multimodal speech enhancement systems.
authors: Khubaib Ahmed, Ahsan Adeel, Nasir Saleem, Kia Dashtipour, Ahsan Ulhaq, Amir Hussain
bullets: Targets computationally expensive audio-visual speech enhancement models for resource-constrained edge devices.
Uses PPO with constraint-aware action masking and a reward balancing SI-SNR improvement with model compactness.
Searches 35 temporally aligned candidate architectures and selects a 2.9M-parameter model versus a 22M-parameter baseline.
The model achieves 14.5 dB SI-SNR improvement, within 0.7 dB of the baseline, with roughly nine-fold lower model size and 4.3× lower real-time factor on mobile CPUs.
Shallower, wider temporal convolutions and aggressive visual-pathway pruning support efficiency; RL-NAS is reported as 92% more search-efficient than random search.
papers.selection_reason: RL-based neural architecture search for compact audio-visual speech enhancement directly targets on-device efficiency and latency reduction.
papers.title: Efficient Audio-Visual Speech Enhancement via Reinforcement Learning-Based Neural Architecture Search
papers.tldr: An RL-driven neural architecture search finds a compact AVSE model that nearly matches baseline enhancement quality while substantially reducing size and mobile inference cost.

papers.abstract: Pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) policies fail on memory tasks, behaviour that depends on events observed long before the current frame, because their training data is overwhelmingly Markov and mapping episodic memory directly to action chunks is hard. Yet the same policy, finetuned once to follow a privileged oracle's grounded-subgoal text, nearly solves these tasks: the difficulty lies entirely in mapping memory to a grounded symbolic subgoal. Existing work entrusts this stage to a single VLM that selects keyframes and reasons over raw frames, and falls far short of the oracle: key identities and dynamics are buried in noisy pixels, the reasoning spans hundreds of frames in an unbounded context, and hallucination corrupts the memory itself. We instead present GAMMA (Grounded multi-Agent Memory with Mechanical Audit), which builds the stage as a collaborating two-agent memory system: a detector tool (SAM-3) for spatial grounding, a VLM writer that distils each replan window into one grounded text line, an append-only text memory bank, and a VLM reasoner that reads the bank and emits the next grounded subgoal at the oracle's cadence, wrapped in a propose-verify harness that admits, defers, corrects, or rejects every agent claim against mechanical visual evidence, at training-corpus construction and at deployment alike. On a sixteen-task memory-manipulation suite GAMMA recovers a large fraction of the oracle ceiling with the policy held fixed, reaching the ceiling on several tasks, and transfers with unchanged contracts to a second benchmark.
authors: Yudong Liu, Yueqian Lin, Zijia Tang, Yuxi Zheng, Yuan Li, Shuai Zhang, Yi Li, Taotao Jing, Shuangjun Liu, Dashan Gao, Ning Bi, Jingwei Sun, Yiran Chen, Hai Helen Li
bullets: Addresses VLA failures on tasks requiring information from events far before the current frame.
Uses SAM-3 for spatial grounding, a VLM writer for concise episodic summaries, and a VLM reasoner to produce grounded subgoals.
Maintains an append-only text memory bank and verifies, corrects, defers, or rejects claims using mechanical visual evidence.
Recovers much of the privileged-oracle performance on a 16-task suite, reaching the oracle ceiling on several tasks.
Transfers to a second benchmark without changing its contracts; performance is scoped to the tested memory-manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Grounded multi-agent memory system with mechanical audit for memory-intensive VLA manipulation.
papers.title: Gamma: Grounded Multi-Agent Memory with Mechanical Audit for Memory-Intensive Manipulation
papers.tldr: GAMMA combines grounded visual detection, structured text memory, multi-agent reasoning, and mechanical verification to help fixed VLA policies solve long-horizon memory-based manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: Reliable robotic manipulation requires maintaining a firm grasp while strictly avoiding both contact slip and structural damage to the object. Satisfying these inherent \textit{secure-and-gentle} grasping constraints is challenging for unknown objects. We present a novel online data-driven predictive control framework for safe dynamic robotic grasping of unknown objects. The proposed system features a pair of compact, single-channel tactile-sensing modules that characterize the gripper-object dynamic interaction in real time, entirely bypassing the need for prior knowledge or offline training. A finite-state-machine-based grasping force probing mechanism is developed to establish the initial grasping force and explicitly identify grasping force constraints. Through online dynamics learning, a Gaussian Process (GP) model captures gripper-object interaction dynamics. The model uncertainties are further used to form robust grasping constraints, which are embedded into a model predictive control scheme. We demonstrate error convergence in a probabilistic sense. The proposed control framework runs at 100~Hz in real time to dynamically manipulate and handle objects rather than static holding. Extensive experimental evaluations across diverse contact surface topologies and various types of objects validate superior performance and efficiency compared to baseline strategies. The proposed method is able to manipulate objects ranging from delicate items, such as raw tofu and marshmallows, to rough objects, such as rocks.
bullets: Uses compact single-channel tactile sensors to monitor gripper–object interactions in real time.
Probes for an initial grasp force and identifies force constraints with a finite-state machine.
Learns interaction dynamics online with a Gaussian Process and incorporates uncertainty into robust MPC constraints.
Runs at 100 Hz and demonstrates probabilistic error convergence during dynamic manipulation.
Experiments cover delicate and rough objects across varied contact surfaces, including tofu, marshmallows, and rocks.
papers.selection_reason: Online data-driven predictive control with tactile sensing for secure and gentle grasping of unknown objects.
papers.title: Tactile Sensing-based Secure and Gentle Grasping of Unknown Objects
papers.tldr: An online tactile-feedback predictive controller enables secure, gentle dynamic grasping of unknown objects without prior models or offline training.

papers.abstract: Self-evolving LLM agents typically improve how they act through accumulated experience, reflection, or skills. Yet even procedurally capable agents can fail when their beliefs about environment dynamics are incomplete, incorrect, or outdated. We study a complementary axis of self-evolution: evolving those beliefs during deployment. Such beliefs can support multiple tasks, but incorrect ones can also propagate across them. We introduce EvoBelief, a self-evolving world model that represents environment knowledge as falsifiable hypotheses. Unexpected outcomes and decision-relevant unknowns trigger hypothesis formation. Later observations and controlled experiments provide independent validation before a rule can guide predictions or plans within its supported scope. Counterexamples narrow or retire rules as the environment changes. The language model remains frozen, and each rule remains linked to its evidence and the decisions it changes. Across four benchmarks spanning static dynamics, hidden drift, and scientific discovery, EvoBelief improves task performance and reuses learned rules across tasks. On ALFWorld without actor-side transition memory, it improves success over the matched Frozen World Model by 23.9% and 31.3% with Claude Haiku 4.5 and GPT-5.4, respectively. On MiniGrid, it revises stale rules and recovers after unannounced dynamics changes. In DiscoveryWorld's Reactor Lab, it discovers and validates quantitative laws, completing 83.3% of Normal-tier and 58.3% of Challenge-tier instances, versus 0% for each evaluated baseline. These results demonstrate self-improvement through testable, revisable environment knowledge rather than model-parameter updates.
authors: Janet Wang, Jiang Guo, Yi Xiang, Jiaqing Yuan, Mingwen Dong, Hideo Kobayashi, Shuaichen Chang, Chandan K. Reddy, Jiarong Jiang
bullets: Targets failures caused by incomplete, incorrect, or outdated beliefs about environment dynamics.
Creates hypotheses from unexpected outcomes or decision-relevant unknowns, then validates them through observations and controlled experiments.
Links each rule to supporting evidence and affected decisions; counterexamples narrow or retire stale rules.
Across four benchmarks, it improves task performance, reuses rules across tasks, adapts to hidden dynamics changes, and discovers quantitative laws.
Reported gains include 23.9% and 31.3% higher ALFWorld success than a matched Frozen World Model, and nonzero DiscoveryWorld completion where baselines achieved 0%.
papers.selection_reason: Self-evolving falsifiable world model for LLM agents; fits world models and deployment-time belief adaptation.
papers.title: EvoBelief: Falsifiable World Models for Self-Improving LLM Agents
papers.tldr: EvoBelief helps frozen LLM agents self-improve by forming, testing, and revising falsifiable world-model hypotheses during deployment.

papers.abstract: Aligning two independently pretrained unimodal encoders typically demands millions of paired examples. In this paper, we study the regime where only $N \sim 100$--$500$ pairs are available, while unpaired data on either side is abundant. Our method expresses every representation by its similarities to the $N$ paired anchors, which places both modalities in a common coordinate system; matches the two point clouds with a single entropic optimal transport problem solved over the entire pool, whose marginal constraints counteract the hubness that defeats nearest-neighbor matching; and distills the resulting plan into two lightweight encoders, so that the correspondence becomes inductive. We additionally put this marginal constraint in relation with the one-step hub corrections of the bilingual lexicon induction literature. Pairing is required only for the anchors: the unpaired collections may be drawn independently from the two marginals, so that no item outside the anchor set needs to have both of its modalities observed. We evaluate on image-text and molecule-text alignment, where our method outperforms existing approaches at the same anchor budget on Flickr30k, MS-COCO and ChEBI-20.
bullets: Targets cross-modal alignment when only about 100–500 paired examples are available.
Represents each item by its similarities to paired anchors, creating a shared coordinate system.
Uses entropic optimal transport with marginal constraints to reduce hubness and match the full representation pools.
Distills the transport plan into lightweight encoders, making the learned correspondence inductive.
Outperforms existing methods at the same anchor budget on image–text and molecule–text benchmarks, including Flickr30k, MS-COCO, and ChEBI-20.
papers.selection_reason: Few-shot multimodal representation alignment via optimal transport; fits multimodal foundation model interests.
papers.title: Representation Alignment from a Few Paired Data via Distilled Optimal Transport
papers.tldr: A few hundred paired anchors plus abundant unpaired data can align independently pretrained encoders by combining anchor-based representations, global entropic optimal transport, and distillation.

papers.abstract: Humans effortlessly react to the world; they adeptly return a tennis shot, catch a falling cup, step aside from a passing cart, or pass a box tossed during truck unloading. These everyday actions require anticipating a moving target and reflexively responding with the whole body within about a second. Such visual reactive whole-body control remains challenging for humanoids, which must (1) coordinate whole-body control, (2) react to object dynamics in real time, and (3) ground perception in egocentric vision. We study catching thrown boxes as a representative task that demands all three capabilities; existing systems cover only part of it, relying on end-effectors, motion capture, or marked objects. We present Reflex, a three-stage framework that learns these capabilities stage by stage while connecting them through a compact representation of object dynamics. First, a state-based policy learns whole-body catching with reinforcement learning. Second, the policy learns to infer the dynamics of a moving box from delayed and incomplete observations. Third, an egocentric RGB-D encoder learns to recover this dynamics representation directly from visual observations while keeping the whole-body controller fixed. This decomposition provides each capability with a direct training signal and makes visual learning substantially more scalable. In simulation, Reflex achieves 85.7% catch success from egocentric RGB-D, compared with 87.9% when given privileged box observations. Temporal visual history is critical: removing it reduces success by 35.6 and 39.8 points on centered and laterally offset throws. On a real Unitree G1, Reflex catches human-thrown boxes with 65% and 40% success at 2.5 and 5 m, reaching 76% and 59% of human catchers' success at the same distances.
authors: Taoyang Jia, Weikai Huang, Linxin Song, Jared Darlington, Jieyu Zhao, Yue Wang, Jiafei Duan, Zhongzheng Ren, Ranjay Krishna
bullets: Addresses the challenge of combining whole-body control, moving-object dynamics prediction, and egocentric visual grounding.
Uses a three-stage framework: reinforcement-learned catching, dynamics inference from delayed observations, and RGB-D perception of that dynamics representation.
In simulation, achieves 85.7% catch success from egocentric RGB-D, close to 87.9% with privileged object observations.
Temporal visual history is essential, with its removal reducing success by 35.6–39.8 percentage points.
On a Unitree G1, catches human-thrown boxes at 65% success from 2.5 m and 40% from 5 m.
papers.selection_reason: Visually grounded reactive whole-body humanoid control via staged RL and egocentric RGB-D perception.
papers.title: Reflex: Visually Grounded Reactive Humanoid Control
papers.tldr: Reflex enables humanoids to visually anticipate and catch moving boxes with coordinated whole-body reactions in real time.

papers.abstract: Foundation models are increasingly used for high-level multi-robot task planning, yet independently generated symbolic plans can become jointly infeasible after geometric grounding because of shared spatial and temporal constraints. We study execution-aware coordination of large-language-model (LLM) planners for multi-robot navigation. We compare a centralized architecture, in which one LLM jointly reasons over the robot team, with a decentralized multi-LLM architecture in which each robot independently proposes a task plan. A geometric verifier grounds the candidate plans into robot trajectories, detects predicted inter-robot conflicts, and converts conflict information into structured feedback for targeted replanning. This verifier-mediated architecture separates semantic task reasoning from execution-level feasibility while enabling iterative coordination among LLM planners. Experiments in CARLA and on Crazyflie aerial robots evaluate coordination performance as task complexity increases and characterize the trade-offs between centralized reasoning, decentralized verifier-mediated coordination, and physical executability.
authors: Vivek Khatana, Zijian Song, Naira Hovakimyan, Petros Voulgaris
bullets: Addresses the gap between independently generated symbolic plans and jointly feasible robot trajectories.
Compares centralized joint planning with decentralized, per-robot LLM planning.
Uses geometric grounding to detect inter-robot spatial and temporal conflicts.
Feeds structured conflict information back to LLM planners for iterative coordination.
Evaluates increasing task complexity in CARLA and with Crazyflie aerial robots, including physical executability trade-offs.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-robot path planning with LLM planners coordinated by a geometric verifier for execution-aware feasibility.
papers.title: Verifier-Mediated Multi-LLM Coordination for Multi-Robot Path Planning
papers.tldr: A geometric verifier helps coordinate centralized or decentralized LLM planners by detecting trajectory conflicts and guiding replanning for feasible multi-robot navigation.

papers.abstract: Ego-trajectory prediction in urban roadway work zones remains an underexplored topic in autonomous-driving research, with limited dedicated data and systematic evaluation. Roadway work zones involve temporary changes in the lane layouts and connectivity of the roads, complicating interactions with surrounding vehicles and workers. These changes make future vehicle trajectories difficult to predict. To address these challenges, we collect WZDrive-Data, a multimodal dataset comprising 1,183 work-zone driving segments from 33 drivers, using a human-in-the-loop driving simulator with prerecorded worker animations and VR-controlled workers. Driver control and gaze signals are recorded from human participants, while vehicle trajectories and scene information are obtained from the simulator. Our proposed multimodal ego-trajectory predictor, WZDrive, achieves a mean minADE (K=6) of 1.09 m and minFDE (K=6) of 2.12 m. Compared with the best-performing state-of-the-art baseline for each metric in our benchmark, WZDrive reduces minADE (K=6) by 7.18% and minFDE (K=6) by 13.18%. This research addresses a gap in autonomous-driving research on urban work zones by combining human-in-the-loop data collection with multimodal learning from human driving signals and in the context of work zones.
authors: Shuo Zhang, Aman Sunesh, Semiha Ergan, Kaan Ozbay
bullets: Work zones introduce temporary lane changes and altered road connectivity, making vehicle-trajectory prediction difficult and underexplored.
The WZDrive-Data dataset contains 1,183 work-zone driving segments from 33 drivers, including vehicle, scene, control, and gaze signals.
The WZDrive predictor uses multimodal human-driving and scene information to forecast multiple possible ego trajectories.
It achieves minADE@6 of 1.09 m and minFDE@6 of 2.12 m, improving on the strongest benchmark baselines by 7.18% and 13.18%, respectively.
The study focuses on urban roadway work zones and relies on human-in-the-loop simulator data.
papers.selection_reason: Learned ego-trajectory prediction for autonomous driving in work zones, fits embodied robot navigation.
papers.title: Trajectory Prediction for Autonomous Driving in Road Construction Zones Using Human-in-the-Loop Driving Data
papers.tldr: WZDrive combines human-in-the-loop work-zone driving data with multimodal prediction to improve autonomous-vehicle ego-trajectory forecasting in complex construction zones.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient continual learning updates a restricted subset of adapter parameters to incorporate sequential tasks while limiting catastrophic forgetting. Gradient attribution is a common rule for selecting that subset, but it requires an additional backward pass over calibration data. We identify a parameter-pool confound in comparisons between initialization-time gradient masks and unrestricted random masks under standard zero-initialized LoRA ($B=0$): the gradient with respect to $A$ is identically zero ($\partial\mathcal{L}/\partial A=0$), so gradient masks select strictly from the $B$ matrix whereas unrestricted random masks draw from both $A$ and $B$. Such a comparison changes both the selection rule and the candidate parameter pool. Isolating the selection criterion by restricting both approaches to the same parameter pool, we find a negative result: a uniform random mask consistently achieves lower loss-based backward transfer than gradient attribution across seven seeds on Qwen2.5-3B. The effect is concentrated on the medical task, which contributes 80\% of the aggregate; code and math move in the same direction, and legal shows no reliable difference. This advantage is consistent with a stability--plasticity trade-off under the tested task sequence, in which random masking slightly reduces single-task fitting. On the two discrete-option tasks (Medical and Legal), the mean accuracy-BWT difference is not statistically distinguishable from zero.
authors: Yu Sun, Junwei Zhou, Zuodong Xiang, Yike Zhang, Pengcheng Xu, Xinyu Guan, Ruoyun Ma, Hailu Xu
bullets: Zero-initialized LoRA makes gradients with respect to A identically zero, causing gradient masks to select only B while unrestricted random masks sample both A and B.
Restricting both methods to the same B-matrix pool isolates the selection rule rather than the candidate-parameter pool.
Across seven seeds on Qwen2.5-3B, random masking consistently produces lower loss-based backward transfer than gradient attribution.
The effect is driven mainly by the medical task; code and math follow the same trend, while legal shows no reliable difference.
On Medical and Legal, mean accuracy-based backward-transfer differences are not statistically distinguishable from zero.
papers.selection_reason: Directly studies continual learning with LoRA and catastrophic forgetting in LLMs.
papers.title: Static Gradient Attribution Underperforms a Density-Matched Random Mask on Loss-Based Forgetting Within LoRA B-Matrix
papers.tldr: Within the LoRA B-matrix, a density-matched uniform random mask yields better loss-based backward transfer than initialization-time gradient attribution under the tested continual-learning setup.

papers.abstract: We interpret Transformer networks as learned approximations to a hybrid probabilistic-inference procedure that combines max-product Loopy Belief Propagation (LBP) with Expectation--Maximization (EM). In this view, a Transformer performs inference in partially observed Markov Random Fields (MRFs) whose structure and parameters are not given a priori but are inferred from data. We show that self-attention implements a differentiable approximation to max-product LBP on an input-conditioned, dynamically structured MRF, with attention weights encoding learned structural affinities. We further establish an EM correspondence at the level of depth: each layer updates latent representations in an E-step-like forward pass, while the transition $\theta^{(l)} \to \theta^{(l+1)}$ across layers acts as an implicit M-step. Building on this interpretation, we introduce \emph{meta-models}, a design paradigm in which inputs generate instance-specific parameters, unifying mechanisms such as self-attention, mixture-of-experts, and gated units within a single framework. Empirical results support the proposed perspective.
bullets: Reinterprets self-attention as differentiable max-product LBP on input-conditioned Markov Random Fields.
Maps Transformer depth to EM: layerwise representation updates resemble E-steps, while parameter transitions resemble implicit M-steps.
Introduces meta-models, where inputs generate instance-specific parameters.
Unifies self-attention, mixture-of-experts, and gated units under this meta-model perspective.
Reports empirical support for the proposed interpretation, without specifying results in the abstract.
papers.selection_reason: Presents a unifying view of Transformer architectures and meta-models, relevant to LLM architecture research.
papers.title: Neural expectation-maximization and meta-models
papers.tldr: Transformers can be viewed as learned, input-adaptive EM and max-product LBP procedures over dynamically structured probabilistic models.

papers.abstract: Indoor navigation to task-relevant targets remains difficult when the target is small, occluded, or visually indistinct. Meanwhile, smart appliances, mobile devices, and IoT tags emit Wi-Fi signals during everyday communication, providing a pervasive but underused spatial cue. We study visual-Wi-Fi navigation, where a robot reaches a signal-emitting device in an unmapped environment using onboard visual observations and Wi-Fi packets overheard from the device, without connecting to the device or modifying infrastructure. Realizing this requires pose-dependent Wi-Fi observations during closed-loop policy learning and reliable spatial cues from bearing measurements corrupted by indoor multipath propagation on a moving robot. We present WiFiSpaces, which extends the Habitat embodied simulator with online ray-traced Wi-Fi sensing, rendering Wi-Fi observations for a robot-mounted antenna array at continuous poses during policy rollouts. On top of it, we build ViFiNav, a localization-aware navigation framework: an online source-localization algorithm exploits robot motion to disambiguate and robustly aggregate bearings from multiple viewpoints into a confidence-aware source estimate, and a learned policy fuses this evolving estimate with depth observations and learns to act on it as it is refined. Experiments show that exploiting robot motion is key to accurate source estimates, and that fine-tuning on ray-traced Wi-Fi observations in WiFiSpaces improves the success rate of ViFiNav. The policy transfers zero-shot to unseen scene datasets, and we deploy it on a real robot with a Wi-Fi sensor built from a commodity router, without any real-world training.
authors: Lihao Wang, Tianjian Xu, Tianmin Shu, Renjie Zhao
bullets: Addresses navigation to small, occluded, or visually indistinct devices using Wi-Fi signals as a spatial cue.
Introduces WiFiSpaces, a Habitat extension that simulates pose-dependent, ray-traced Wi-Fi observations during policy rollouts.
Uses robot motion to aggregate noisy multi-view bearing measurements into a confidence-aware source estimate.
A learned policy fuses the evolving Wi-Fi estimate with depth observations for closed-loop navigation.
Improves with ray-traced Wi-Fi fine-tuning, transfers zero-shot to unseen scenes, and runs on a real robot without real-world training.
papers.selection_reason: Learned robot navigation to signal-emitting devices using visual and Wi-Fi observations, with online source localization and policy learning.
papers.title: Visual-Wi-Fi Navigation to Signal-Emitting Devices
papers.tldr: ViFiNav enables robots to navigate unmapped indoor environments to Wi-Fi-emitting devices by combining motion-based source localization, depth vision, and Wi-Fi sensing without infrastructure changes.

papers.abstract: Parameter-efficient fine-tuning has hundreds of methods, usually compared by parameter count and benchmark score. We compare them as maps. A pretrained checkpoint is a base point in weight space, and a weight-space method is a smooth map from a small parameter space that starts at that point. These maps form a slice category in which the frozen model is initial and full fine-tuning terminal. Three invariants of the map do most of the work. Its image near the base point governs expressivity, through the first-order image, the dimension, a min-cut bound on rank and whether that point is smooth or an apex. Its fibres, with the optimizer's metric, govern training dynamics. Base change moves the base point and covers splitting initialisations, quantisation, restarts and merging. We prove, for example, that zero-initialised LoRA, and Householder reflection adaptation at its default start under stated rank and parity conditions, begin at the apex of a cone; that no exact initialisation lets LoRA reach an update of rank above twice its own; that exactly orthogonal methods never change a weight's singular values in exact arithmetic, however often they are merged; that under Adam with no epsilon, weight decay or clipping and one shared schedule, LoRA+ from the standard zero initialisation follows exactly the trajectory of plain LoRA with its scale multiplied by the learning-rate ratio; that Adam with shared hyperparameters respects only the signed permutations inside LoRA's continuous symmetry group of full-rank factors; and that the activation function decides when a scaling adapter folds into preceding weights. We classify 382 methods from 138 papers by seven coordinates read off their formulas, with 403 simulation arrows and 485 obstructions. Every numbered result is proved in full, and results due to others are credited where we re-derive them.
authors: Xiaoyu Li, Zhizhou Sha, Chiwun Yang, Dai Shi
bullets: Models fine-tuning methods as smooth maps from low-dimensional parameter spaces into weight space, forming a slice category from frozen to full fine-tuning.
Characterizes methods using image geometry, fibres with optimizer metrics, and base changes such as quantization, restarts, splitting, and merging.
Proves structural results for LoRA, Householder adaptation, orthogonal methods, LoRA+, Adam symmetries, and scaling adapters.
Classifies 382 methods from 138 papers using seven formula-derived coordinates, supported by 403 simulation arrows and 485 obstructions.
Results often depend on stated assumptions, including initialization, rank and parity, optimizer settings, exact arithmetic, and activation functions.
papers.selection_reason: Theoretical analysis of parameter-efficient fine-tuning as adaptation methods, transferable to continual/test-time adaptation.
papers.title: A Categorical Atlas of Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning: Cones, Orbits, and Gauges
papers.tldr: This paper provides a categorical framework for comparing parameter-efficient fine-tuning methods through their geometry, symmetries, and training dynamics rather than parameter counts alone.

papers.abstract: Feed-forward 3D foundation models reconstruct scenes from unposed images, but the quadratic cost of global attention limits their scalability to large view sets. We present Zebra3D, a layerwise sparse-linear hybrid attention framework that improves the efficiency of pretrained 3D foundation models without training from scratch. Across VGGT, HunyuanWorld-Mirror, and $\pi^3$, we observe a broadly consistent depth-wise pattern: early stages are relatively tolerant to linear replacement, while sensitive middle-to-late stages tend to exhibit more concentrated attention. Zebra3D exploits this structure by assigning linear-centered attention to tolerant stages and tile-sparse attention to sensitive stages, using landmark summaries to preserve unselected context. Closed-form affine fitting enables training-free conversion, while optional post-conversion training combines task supervision with output and relational feature distillation. Across all three backbones, Zebra3D achieves strong reconstruction and camera-pose accuracy at high attention sparsity, with training-free variants remaining close to their dense counterparts. End-to-end speedups increase with input view count, reaching up to $7.1\times$ at 1,024 views. After post-conversion training, Zebra3D-VGGT reaches 80.5\% RealEstate10K AUC@30 at 94\% mean attention sparsity, within 1.1 percentage points of dense VGGT fine-tuned on the same data and schedule.
authors: Utkarsh Saxena, Ruijing Yang, Mehdi Rezagholizadeh, Akash Haridas, Vikram Appia, Emad Barsoum
bullets: Addresses the quadratic cost of global attention in feed-forward 3D foundation models for unposed-image reconstruction.
Assigns linear-centered attention to tolerant early stages and tile-sparse attention with landmark summaries to sensitive middle-to-late stages.
Converts models without training from scratch using closed-form affine fitting; optional distillation-based post-conversion training further improves performance.
Across VGGT, HunyuanWorld-Mirror, and π³, maintains strong reconstruction and camera-pose accuracy at high attention sparsity.
Zebra3D-VGGT reaches 80.5% RealEstate10K AUC@30 at 94% mean sparsity, within 1.1 percentage points of dense fine-tuned VGGT; speedup reaches 7.1× at 1,024 views.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a layerwise sparse-linear hybrid attention framework to improve the scalability of 3D foundation models, directly addressing efficiency in 3D reconstruction.
papers.title: Zebra3D: Efficient Hybrid Foundation Models For Scalable 3D Reconstruction
papers.tldr: Zebra3D makes pretrained 3D reconstruction models scalable to many views by replacing dense attention with layerwise hybrid sparse-linear attention, achieving up to 7.1× speedup with limited accuracy loss.

papers.abstract: Neural surrogates that forecast a physical field from sparse, noisy sensors read a window of nearby sensors and a history of past snapshots. Practitioners choose both by comparing fitted models with each other. Such comparisons cannot tell a model's shortfall from missing information. We measure the trade-off between window and history against the Bayes-optimal error of the same readings. An exact Gaussian analysis shows that noisy or sparse observation of a field with local dynamics makes the optimal forecast read distant sensors only through spatial correlation. On a forced linear field with a known optimum, trained models that read only the window come within 1% of it. We then train such models on viscous Burgers flow and the chaotic Kuramoto-Sivashinsky (KS) equation, with every deciding comparison fixed before any test evaluation. In every field except KS, eight snapshots remove a smaller fraction of the one-snapshot error as the lead time, the number of steps to the forecast target, grows. In KS, for windows up to one correlation length, they remove a larger fraction. This lead-time inversion persists across sensor densities, three architectures and a two-dimensional domain. It shrinks as damping lowers the Lyapunov exponent. Damping also removes the linear instability of KS. We therefore tie the inversion to instability and leave chaos and linear amplification unseparated. For surrogate design the results give two rules. Size the window in correlation lengths of the field. Split a fixed input budget between window and history for the lead time the model will serve, because the best split moves toward wider windows as the lead time grows. In Burgers flow the split chosen at lead time one ends with 13.5 times the best error at lead time eight.
bullets: Bayes-optimal analysis finds that distant sensors help mainly through spatial correlation when observations are sparse or noisy.
For a forced linear field, window-only models approach the known optimum, coming within 1%.
In most tested fields, history becomes relatively less useful at longer lead times; chaotic Kuramoto–Sivashinsky flow shows the opposite for short windows.
The lead-time inversion persists across sensor densities, architectures, and a two-dimensional domain, but weakens with damping.
Choosing the input split for one-step forecasting can be highly suboptimal at longer horizons; in Burgers flow, it yields 13.5× the best error at lead time eight.
papers.selection_reason: Studies input context sizing for neural predictors of physical field dynamics, relevant to world model design.
papers.title: Spatial Context or Memory? Sizing the Inputs of Neural Surrogates for Partially Observed Fields
papers.tldr: The study shows how to size spatial windows and temporal history in neural surrogates for partially observed physical fields, with the best balance depending on forecast lead time and field instability.

papers.abstract: Large language models are stochastic by nature. Repeated executions under the same experimental conditions may produce different responses. We propose a framework that can be applied across the model lifecycle, from task design to residual behavior and continuous monitoring. The method consists of building an empirical response distribution estimated through Monte Carlo simulation. Semantic interventions are introduced to study how these distributions change. We illustrate the framework with two different tasks, borrower classification and music album recommendation, and quantify the resulting distributional changes. The framework is linked to model risk management and governance by measuring robustness and control effectiveness, and characterizing residual behavior. Since it relies only on observed responses, it can also be applied to black-box models accessed through commercial APIs.
bullets: Addresses variability in LLM outputs across repeated executions under identical conditions.
Estimates response distributions via Monte Carlo simulation across the model lifecycle.
Uses semantic interventions to measure changes in behavioral distributions.
Demonstrates the approach on borrower classification and music album recommendation tasks.
Connects distributional measurements to robustness, control effectiveness, governance, and residual behavior.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a distributional framework for characterizing LLM behavior and risk management, fitting the 'Language Foundation Models' topic.
papers.title: A Distributional Framework for Behavioral Characterization and Risk Management of Large Language Models
papers.tldr: A black-box-compatible framework uses empirical response distributions to characterize, test, and manage the stochastic behavior and risks of large language models.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon manipulation requires robots to retain task-relevant history while revising conclusions no longer supported by physical evidence. Retaining observations alone does not specify which completed conditions should be withdrawn after a disturbance or which obligations require repair. We introduce REMM, Revisable Embodied Memory for Manipulation, a supervisory memory layer for a frozen G0.5 vision-language-action executor. REMM separates an append-only evidence history from revisable task state and explicitly links derived relations and completed conditions to their supporting facts. When accepted evidence changes a supporting fact, it withdraws dependent conclusions and schedules targeted recovery at verified skill boundaries without updating the executor. Across 51 physical trials, including operator-assisted runs, REMM improves mean recorded task progress over the strongest baseline from 57% to 91% in intervention recovery and from 43% to 70% in sequence recall. Complementary video diagnostics show improved grounding of retained history into the next instruction, including comparisons with $\pi_{0.5}$-compatible high-level planner adaptations. These results support revisable memory as a practical interface for continued manipulation without policy retraining. Project: https://revanthsenthil.github.io/remm/.
authors: Revanth Krishna Senthilkumaran, Ruwan Wickramarachchi, Alessandro Oltramari, Jonathan Francis
bullets: Targets long-horizon manipulation, where robots must retain useful history while retracting unsupported conclusions.
Uses a supervisory memory layer for a frozen G0.5 vision-language-action executor, without policy retraining.
Links derived relations and completed conditions to supporting facts, then withdraws affected conclusions when evidence changes.
Schedules targeted recovery at verified skill boundaries after disturbances.
Across 51 physical trials, mean recorded progress improved from 57% to 91% for intervention recovery and from 43% to 70% for sequence recall.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces revisable embodied memory layer for manipulation with frozen VLA executor, directly fitting embodied memory and robot manipulation.
papers.title: REMM: Revisable Embodied Memory for Manipulation
papers.tldr: REMM helps robots recover from manipulation disturbances by maintaining evidence separately from revisable task state and repairing only conclusions invalidated by new evidence.

papers.abstract: Vision-language reward models are trained on annotated preference pairs, which are expensive to collect, can disagree, and are ranked by benchmark accuracy. We build one with no human preference label: a linear head on an intermediate layer of a frozen Qwen3-VL backbone, trained to score a web caption above a perturbed version of the same caption; labeled data enters only to select the layer. The layer is the decisive choice, worth 5.8 points over the last layer, and one recipe transferred without re-tuning beats or at least matches GPT-4o on three benchmarks at 32B, 6.6 points ahead on VL-RewardBench, from a few thousand parameters at about a thousandth of fine-tuning compute. At an equal pair budget, perturbations teach a frozen head 3 to 5 points more than curated RLAIF-V pairs. Because the backbone is frozen, the objective is convex, and the perturbation sampler specifies the reward, which the benchmark does not identify: two heads trained on disjoint halves of the same perturbations tie on the benchmark and differ by 6.4 points in hallucination judging. Retraining the head on the policy's own verifier-labeled candidates cuts caption hallucination by 5.1 CHAIR points and lifts image-generation pass rate by 5.4, while scoring lower on every reward benchmark. Together, an intermediate-layer probe, free same-image perturbations, and a verifier-driven bootstrap turn give a recipe for multimodal reward modeling that needs no annotator, costs a fraction of fine-tuning, and is specified by the comparisons it is trained on rather than by a benchmark rank.
authors: Yueying Li, Jingxuan Fan, Kiant\'e Brantley, Sham M. Kakade, Hanlin Zhang
bullets: Uses a linear head over a frozen Qwen3-VL intermediate layer, training original web captions to outrank perturbed versions.
Selecting the intermediate layer is critical, improving performance by 5.8 points over using the last layer.
A single recipe matches or exceeds GPT-4o across three benchmarks at 32B and leads VL-RewardBench by 6.6 points.
With equal pair budgets, perturbation-based training outperforms curated RLAIF-V pairs by 3–5 points.

Benchmark scores do not fully identify reward behavior: perturbation choice affects hallucination judgments, while verifier-driven bootstrapping improves CHAIR and image-generation pass rate despite lower benchmark scores.
papers.selection_reason: Unsupervised vision-language reward modeling on frozen VLM, relevant to multimodal foundation models.
papers.title: Unsupervised Multimodal Reward Modeling
papers.tldr: An unsupervised intermediate-layer reward head trained on caption perturbations can provide low-cost, task-specific multimodal rewards without human preference labels.

papers.abstract: Vision-language-action models (VLAs) offer a promising route toward general-purpose robotics by transferring semantic knowledge from large-scale vision-language pretraining into language-conditioned control. However, most VLA evaluations emphasize aggregate manipulation success under changes in objects, instructions, or environments, leaving unclear how reliably these policies ground spatial descriptions in the physical scenes where they act. We therefore ask a sharper question: how reliably can current VLAs translate spatial descriptions into appropriate real-robot behavior? To investigate this, we introduce Spa-Bench, a real-robot benchmark that evaluates spatial grounding across six tabletop tasks covering Object State, Relative Size, Referential Description, Relational Placement, Ordinal Position, and Counting. Our primary evaluation compares in-distribution (ID) and out-of-distribution (OOD) spatial configurations while retaining training support for the relevant objects, concepts, and actions, reducing object and motor unfamiliarity as alternative explanations for failure. Four diagnostic conditions further probe physical execution, sensitivity to wording, object-task associations, and recognition that no action is required. We release 4,092 episodes collected on the SO-101 robot arm: 1,200 human-teleoperated demonstrations and 2,892 real-robot evaluation rollouts from five state-of-the-art VLA policies. Across the three fully evaluated policies, success falls from 67.5-73.3% on ID spatial configurations to 40.7-52.0% on OOD spatial configurations, while matched direct instructions improve success by 28.3-40.0 percentage points. These results show that the evaluated VLAs can often execute the required manipulations but lack robust spatial grounding. Project materials, including videos, code, and benchmark data, are available at https://justintiensmith.github.io/Spa-Bench/.
authors: Justin Tien-Smith, Matthew Pidden, Rolandos Alexandros Potamias
bullets: Introduces a real-robot benchmark spanning six tabletop spatial tasks: object state, relative size, referential description, relational placement, ordinal position, and counting.
Compares in-distribution and out-of-distribution spatial configurations while controlling for object and motor unfamiliarity.
Adds diagnostics for physical execution, wording sensitivity, object-task associations, and recognizing when no action is needed.
Evaluates 4,092 episodes on the SO-101 robot arm, including demonstrations and rollouts from five VLA policies.

Across three fully evaluated policies, success drops from 67.5–73.3% on in-distribution configurations to 40.7–52.0% on out-of-distribution configurations; direct instructions improve success by 28.3–40.0 percentage points.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark evaluating spatial grounding of VLA policies on real robot, directly fitting vision-language-action and manipulation.
papers.title: Spa-Bench: A Real-Robot Benchmark for Spatial Grounding in Vision-Language-Action Models
papers.tldr: Spa-Bench shows that current vision-language-action models often execute manipulations but struggle to reliably ground spatial descriptions in real-world scenes.

papers.abstract: Non-prehensile manipulation with mobile robots has primarily targeted placement in coarse goal regions. Precision placement has been studied with manipulators on benchmarks such as Push-T, where an omnidirectional end effector can readily re-approach an object from any side. For a mobile robot, correcting the same placement errors may require wide repositioning maneuvers around the object. We formalize multi-object pushing with a mobile robot as a multi-target assignment problem at tight tolerances. We propose a diffusion planner with a causal factorization: each robot denoising step is followed by an object step conditioned on the current clean robot estimate. This factorization allows us to sample multiple object outcomes for a single robot plan, capturing the multi-modality of pushing. We also design a set of pushing-specific costs for mobile robots, used for both guidance and best-of-$N$ sampling at inference. On Push-T, our planner attains the highest success rate of the methods we compare, while having the lowest rate of implausible object motion. Across three multi-box pushing environments resembling warehouse scenarios, it raises the fraction of boxes placed by $21.5$ percentage points over an unguided baseline, and replans $1.8\times$ faster than a planner that denoises the two trajectories together. Lastly, we deploy the guided planner on a TurtleBot 3 Burger with object shapes absent from the training data, where it places $85.0\%$ of objects within tolerance against Diffusion Policy's $37.5\%$.
authors: Lance Pharand, Megnath Ramesh, Mark Chiu, Yash Vardhan Pant, Stephen L. Smith
bullets: Formulates tight-tolerance multi-object pushing as a multi-target assignment problem for mobile robots.
Uses causal diffusion: each robot denoising step is followed by an object step conditioned on the robot estimate, capturing multiple possible pushing outcomes.
Introduces pushing-specific costs for guidance and best-of-N trajectory selection.
Achieves the highest compared success rate and lowest implausible-motion rate on Push-T; improves box placement by 21.5 percentage points over an unguided baseline.
Replans 1.8× faster than joint trajectory denoising and places 85.0% of objects within tolerance on a TurtleBot 3 Burger with unseen shapes.
papers.selection_reason: Diffusion-based trajectory planning for non-prehensile mobile manipulation, directly fitting learned robot manipulation.
papers.title: Non-Prehensile Multi-Object Placement with Mobile Robots via Diffusion-Based Trajectory Planning
papers.tldr: A diffusion-based planner enables mobile robots to precisely push and place multiple objects by modeling robot and object trajectories separately with task-specific guidance.

papers.abstract: Large language models are becoming central to GeoAI systems, yet their evaluation rarely considers the elicitation of geospatial data requirements. This omission is critical as retrieval oriented geo-analytic tasks cannot be supported reliably without first identifying the necessary datasets and constraints. GeoFitBench-LLM is introduced as a benchmark for assessing whether LLMs can infer the datasets, the supporting resources and the constraints required by geo-analytic requests in natural language. The benchmark is structured around two reasoning dimensions, Spatio-Temporal Relational and Semantic Grounding, reflecting long-standing challenges in geospatial information retrieval and related natural language tasks. Ground truth requirements are encoded in a fixed, provider-independent schema for reproducible evaluation of resource identification and attribute-level specification. Experiments on seven models under minimal prompting indicate that identifying the necessary resources is often achievable, with GPT-5.4 Thinking achieving the best result by recovering the complete set of resources in 66.67% of benchmark requests. Results further indicate that accurate fitness-for-use specification remains more difficult as inferential demands increase.
authors: Amirhossein Vahdat, Thierry Badard, Luc Lamontagne
bullets: Targets a gap in LLM evaluation: geospatial data-requirements elicitation for retrieval-oriented analysis.
Evaluates two reasoning dimensions: Spatio-Temporal Relational and Semantic Grounding.
Uses a fixed, provider-independent schema to encode ground-truth resource and attribute requirements.
In minimal-prompt experiments across seven models, GPT-5.4 Thinking recovered all required resources for 66.67% of requests.
Resource identification was more achievable than accurate fitness-for-use specification, especially when inference demands increased.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark for LLM geospatial data requirements elicitation, relevant to spatial reasoning evaluation.
papers.title: GeoFitBench-LLM: A Benchmark for Assessing Large Language Models' Capabilities in Geospatial Data Requirements Elicitation for Geo-Analytic Tasks
papers.tldr: GeoFitBench-LLM benchmarks how well LLMs identify the geospatial datasets, resources, and constraints needed for natural-language geo-analytic tasks.

papers.abstract: Language model agents increasingly operate over long interaction streams, requiring online adaptation to distribution shifts through continual learning. However, existing agent harnesses typically either evolve their states only through forward information flow or rely on additional replay or validation data for harness optimization. To address this, we propose ReHarness, a recurrent harness framework for agentic continual learning that complements forward read and write with backward revision under a strictly online streaming protocol. We ask what information could have been captured differently in the harness state to better inform the current instance in the stream. Specifically, after each instance, we leverage the resulting trajectory as feedback to revise the reflections retrieved for that instance, thereby propagating feedback backward through the textual harness state. Across three continual learning benchmarks and three language model backbones, ReHarness consistently outperforms strong raw-context baselines, memory- and reflection-based methods, and prompt optimization approaches. Further analysis shows that ReHarness produces source-grounded and meaningful revisions, corrects overgeneralized or outdated experience under distribution shifts, and improves both stability and plasticity during continual learning.
authors: Yuxin Xiao, Zhiyun Lu, Jianyu Wang, Yangtian Zhang, Yang Song, Qifan Wang, Bailin Wang
bullets: Addresses adaptation to distribution shifts in long, streaming agent interactions.
Adds backward revision to the usual forward read/write updates of agent harnesses.
Uses each completed trajectory to revise the reflections retrieved for the current instance, without replay or validation data.
Outperforms several baseline families across three benchmarks and three language-model backbones.
Revisions are source-grounded, correct outdated or overgeneralized experience, and improve stability–plasticity balance.
papers.selection_reason: Recurrent harness for agentic continual learning under online streaming, directly fits continual/online learning.
papers.title: Recurrent Harness for Agentic Continual Learning
papers.tldr: ReHarness improves online continual learning for language-model agents by revising prior harness reflections using feedback from each new interaction.

papers.abstract: We introduce iRAG, a human-in-the-loop decision-support system combining Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) with Hybrid Decision-Making. Unlike conventional RAG systems, relying on static Knowledge Bases (KBs), our proposal addresses settings where the KB is initially empty and is progressively populated through human decisions. The system stores previous decisions as retrievable precedents and moves from silent observation to evidence-grounded contestation and, finally, to autonomous handling with abstention. Against an independent baseline, iRAG matches final-decision error under 10% drift without retrieval decay and reduces it under 40% drift across all configurations. Retrieval decay improves performance on changed knowledge while increasing error on stable knowledge, evidencing a stability--plasticity trade-off rather than a general advantage. Human oversight is an architectural provision of the workflow; its usability with real human users remains to be evaluated.
bullets: Addresses decision support when the initial knowledge base is empty and populated progressively through human decisions.
Stores prior decisions as retrievable precedents and transitions from observation to contestation to autonomous handling with abstention.
Matches an independent baseline under 10% knowledge drift and reduces error under 40% drift across configurations.
Retrieval decay helps with changed knowledge but harms performance on stable knowledge, revealing a stability–plasticity trade-off.
The workflow includes human oversight, but usability with real users has not yet been evaluated.
papers.selection_reason: Incremental RAG with dynamically populated external memory, relevant to LLM memory and online adaptation.
papers.title: Incremental Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Human-in-the-Loop Decision Support
papers.tldr: iRAG incrementally builds a retrieval base from human decisions to support increasingly autonomous, evidence-grounded decision-making under changing knowledge.

papers.abstract: Efficient autoregressive generation is increasingly limited by the memory footprint of the key-value (KV) cache, which grows linearly with sequence length, batch size, and model depth. Existing approaches such as Multi-Query Attention (MQA), Grouped-Query Attention (GQA), Multi-Head Latent Attention (MLA), and Tensor Product Attention (TPA) reduce this cost through different trade-offs, but often sacrifice expressivity, require additional positional-encoding machinery, or impose restrictive low-rank structure. We propose Kronecker Product Attention (KPA), which represents key and value activations as sums of Kronecker products of compact, token-dependent matrix factors. KPA strictly generalizes TPA: rank-one vector-outer-product factorization arises as a degenerate Kronecker split, while non-degenerate matrix factors can represent richer block-structured patterns. We further show that a structured rotary embedding operator matched to the Kronecker representation preserves the relative-position property of RoPE while rotating only the compact factors, removing the need for a decoupled RoPE branch as in MLA. Empirically, KPA matches or exceeds TPA, MHA, MQA, GQA, and MLA across four model scales and nine downstream benchmarks under identical training conditions, while achieving up to 10x KV cache compression. The Kronecker head split is a tuneable hyperparameter that allows practitioners to navigate the compression-accuracy trade-off at design time without architectural changes.
authors: Bahareh Nikpour, Hossein Rajabzadeh, Maryam Dialameh, Vahid Partovi Nia, Parsa Omidi
bullets: Targets KV-cache memory growth with sequence length, batch size, and model depth.
Represents key/value activations as sums of Kronecker products, strictly generalizing Tensor Product Attention.
Introduces a matched structured rotary embedding that preserves RoPE’s relative-position property without a separate positional branch.
Matches or exceeds several attention baselines across four model scales and nine benchmarks, with up to 10× KV-cache compression.
A tunable Kronecker head split controls the compression–accuracy trade-off without architectural changes.
papers.selection_reason: KV cache compression via structured Kronecker factorization, directly relevant to efficient inference.
papers.title: Kronecker Product Attention: Memory-Efficient KV Compression via Structured Factorization
papers.tldr: Kronecker Product Attention compresses autoregressive KV caches by factorizing keys and values into compact, token-dependent Kronecker factors while preserving positional information and attention expressivity.

papers.abstract: Motion retargeting is a critical preprocessing step for transferring human motion data to humanoid robots. While existing methods are effective for single-character motions, interactions involving multiple characters and objects introduce additional contacts and spatial relationships that must be preserved. Retargeting is commonly formulated as a weighted multi-objective optimization problem, where conflicting objectives can require careful tuning of relative weights and can still compromise important motion characteristics. We introduce PriMoRetarget, a prioritized motion-retargeting framework that replaces relative objective weighting with an explicit priority hierarchy. Lower-priority updates are constrained to preserve higher-priority objectives, allowing critical characteristics such as foot placement and interaction contacts to take precedence over lower-priority pose objectives. The method is evaluated on four datasets spanning single-character motion, character-object manipulation, and character-character interactions. The resulting motions better preserve task-relevant interactions and provide reference trajectories that can be tracked more reliably than those produced by widely used retargeting methods.
authors: Nicholas Ioannidis, Dun Yang, Max Smith, Tue Vu, Ziyu Zhang, Shayegan Omidshafiei, Xue Bin Peng
bullets: Addresses motion-retargeting failures in multi-character and character-object interactions, where contacts and spatial relationships must be preserved.
Replaces manually tuned weighted objectives with prioritized optimization: lower-priority updates cannot compromise higher-priority objectives.
Prioritizes task-critical features such as foot placement and interaction contacts over lower-priority pose matching.
Evaluated across four datasets covering single-character motion, manipulation, and character-character interactions.
Produces motions that better preserve interactions and yield more reliably trackable reference trajectories than widely used retargeting methods.
papers.selection_reason: Prioritized motion retargeting for humanoid robots, relevant to robot skill/control pipelines though not learning-based.
papers.title: PriMoRetarget: Humanoid Motion Transfer Through Prioritized Motion Retargeting
papers.tldr: PriMoRetarget transfers humanoid motion by enforcing a priority hierarchy that preserves critical contacts and spatial relationships over less important pose objectives.

papers.abstract: Recently, soft robotic procedures are being developed aiming at achieving targeted minimally invasive operations or drug administration in specific locations in the human body. Accordingly, specialized path-planning algorithms need to be investigated for the estimation of efficient paths that would protect the delicate tissue structures and simultaneously satisfy a set of requirements for the efficient navigation of the robot. In this context, we propose an image-based 3D pathplanning algorithm, which is an extension of the A* algorithm, for the navigation of a soft-growing robot inside the spinal subarachnoid space (SSS). The proposed algorithm is capable of estimating a safe pathway towards the goal location, while ensuring the establishment of anchor points that facilitate the efficient steering of the soft robot. The algorithm is evaluated using a highly detailed model of the SSS with respect to its capacity to satisfy the robot movement requirements and path efficiency.
authors: George Dimas, Panagiotis G. Kalozoumis, Panagiotis Vartholomeos, Dimitris K. Iakovidis
bullets: Targets minimally invasive procedures and drug delivery in delicate anatomical environments.
Plans paths while accounting for tissue protection and soft-robot navigation requirements.
Establishes anchor points to support effective steering of the growing robot.
Evaluated in a highly detailed spinal subarachnoid space model for movement feasibility and path efficiency.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes image-based 3D path planning for soft-growing robot navigation, directly relevant to robot navigation/planning.
papers.title: Image-Based Path-Planning for Navigation of Soft-Growing Robots in the Spinal Sub-Arachnoid Space
papers.tldr: An image-based 3D extension of A* plans safe, efficient routes for soft-growing robots navigating the spinal subarachnoid space.

papers.abstract: Physics foundation models are an increasingly popular approach for building versatile emulators for spatiotemporal systems. They require tokenisation layers that lift physical field data into a latent representation suitable for dynamic processing. A typical choice for this layer is a convolutional encoder, which lifts field information in a locality-aware way and can be trained very efficiently. However, this choice cannot be applied to a large class of scientific computing problems where data are represented on unstructured meshes, for example simulations on domains with curved boundaries. Such data typically require graph neural network architectures, which are more expensive to train and, in the form currently used, encode information differently from their CNN counterparts, thus limiting the portability of physics emulators between these data regimes. In this work we introduce Mesh-Native Convolution (MNC), a locality-aware tokenisation layer that encodes unstructured mesh-based data in a way that is analogous to CNNs. This approach leads to models that can be trained once on mesh data and then deployed to arbitrary unstructured meshes, even if these are irregular, with minimal retraining. We show that this tokenisation approach can be used to retrofit grid-pretrained foundation models efficiently on unstructured meshes and provide theoretical results to confirm the consistency of this approach with classical CNN encoders. We demonstrate the favourable performance of this retrofitting approach, which in many cases reaches acceptable accuracy even in zero-shot deployment, and outperforms existing baselines after only a few epochs of fine-tuning, thus providing an efficient bridge between the two data regimes.
authors: Georg Maierhofer, Miles Cranmer, Payel Mukhopadhyay
bullets: Unstructured meshes arise in scientific problems such as simulations with curved boundaries, but standard CNN tokenisers are limited to regular grids.
The proposed Mesh-Native Convolution (MNC) provides locality-aware, CNN-analogous tokenisation for mesh-based data.
Models trained on mesh data can be deployed across arbitrary irregular meshes with minimal retraining.
MNC can retrofit grid-pretrained foundation models to unstructured meshes, achieving acceptable accuracy in some zero-shot settings and outperforming baselines after brief fine-tuning.
The approach is supported by theoretical consistency results with classical CNN encoders.
papers.selection_reason: Mesh-native tokenisation for physics foundation models; relevant to world models for spatiotemporal systems.
papers.title: Mesh-Native Tokenisation: Retrofitting Foundation Models to Unstructured Data
papers.tldr: Mesh-Native Convolution adapts CNN-style tokenisation to unstructured meshes, enabling grid-pretrained physics foundation models to transfer efficiently with little or no retraining.

papers.abstract: Humanoid and service robots operating in clut- tered human environments may encounter motion planning problems that are infeasible when all surrounding objects are treated as fixed obstacles. The Minimum Constraint Removal problem, which we refer to as MCR, addresses this situation by identifying the minimum number of constraints, such as movable objects, whose removal enables a collision-free path. However, computing an optimal MCR solution is NP-hard. In this work, we propose a graph-based heuristic pipeline that combines bidirectional feasible-set generation with fixed- length searches over reduced MCR graphs. We further derive an extended feasible-set generator for instances in which the candidates produced by the first generator do not contain a complete optimal removal set. Across six benchmarks, the evaluated pipeline matches the exact solution in three cases and, in the remaining cases, selects at most 31.25% more obstacles than the optimum, while being between 3.4 and 33.7 times faster than exact search. In one of the benchmarks, involving a manipulation task amidst clutter, selecting two rather than seven obstructing objects reduces the combined MCR, inverse- kinematics, and motion planning time from 84.72 s to 30.59 s. These results indicate that the proposed approach provides a practical compromise between computational efficiency and solution quality for motion planning among movable obstacles.
authors: Antony Thomas, Fulvio Mastrogiovanni, Marco Baglietto
bullets: Targets Minimum Constraint Removal (MCR), which is NP-hard in cluttered environments with movable obstacles.
Combines bidirectional feasible-set generation, fixed-length searches, and an extended generator for difficult instances.
Matches the exact solution on three of six benchmarks; other solutions remove at most 31.25% more obstacles than optimal.
Runs 3.4–33.7× faster than exact search and substantially reduces planning time in a cluttered manipulation example.
papers.selection_reason: Addresses motion planning among movable obstacles for humanoid/service robots, fitting learned/planning navigation in cluttered environments.
papers.title: Graph-Based Heuristics for Minimum Constraint Removal in Cluttered Robot Motion Planning
papers.tldr: A graph-based heuristic efficiently finds near-minimal obstacle removals to make otherwise infeasible robot motion plans possible.

papers.abstract: Continual learning (CL) seeks to adapt pretrained models while preserving prior capabilities. Yet the tasks supplied for preservation cover only part of what a model knows, while forgetting can extend beyond them. Recent work shows that language models can supplement this limited evidence by generating useful replay without access to their original training data. This raises a question about self-preservation: can a model help choose preservation targets that protect its own capabilities more broadly? To study this question, we organize task descriptions and their examples into Task Banks, whose entries can be selected and combined to guide replay generation by a frozen model. Continual instruction tuning with Qwen models of varying sizes yields three findings. First, the new task and learning rate shape which prior capabilities degrade, while tracking previously correct answers reveals losses that average accuracy can conceal. Second, generated replay reduces forgetting on tasks outside the bank. Combining partial banks strengthens this protection, improving mean retention of previously correct answers over either bank alone across the tested sizes. Third, the model can also help choose replay targets: selection informed by the new task improves mean held-out retention over random selection at 4B, with similar new-task gains, although smaller models show no corresponding advantage. Under a fixed example budget, however, replacing new-task examples with replay improves preservation at the cost of smaller new-task gains. Together, these findings show that models can support broader self-preservation by generating replay data and, in some settings, choosing which tasks to replay.
authors: Dongkyu Cho, Rumi Chunara, Ali Behrouz
bullets: Continual learning may forget capabilities not represented in the available preservation tasks.
Task Banks organize task descriptions and examples to guide replay generation by a frozen model.
Generated replay reduces forgetting on held-out tasks, and combining partial banks improves retention across tested Qwen model sizes.
New-task-informed replay selection outperforms random selection at 4B, but smaller models show no comparable benefit.
Using a fixed example budget, more replay improves preservation while reducing gains on the new task.
papers.selection_reason: Continual learning with replay for LLM self-preservation; fits continual learning and LLM topics.
papers.title: Self-Preservation in Language Models
papers.tldr: Language models can use generated replay—and sometimes select replay targets—to preserve capabilities beyond the tasks explicitly monitored during continual learning.

papers.abstract: Sparse computation can scale the parametric capacity of LLMs without proportionally increasing active computation, but pretraining sparse architectures remains expensive and data-hungry. Existing sparse upcycling methods mainly target Mixture-of-Experts models, where expert homogeneity, sample inefficiency, and system overheads can limit practical scalability. Static sparse memory offers predictable access and token-specific updates that can help address these challenges, but naively integrating it into pretrained computation yields poor returns. In this work, we introduce STAPLE, a recipe built upon STEM for integrating static sparse memory into pretrained models. Whereas STEM replaces FFN up-projections with token-indexed embeddings, STAPLE retains them and adds the embeddings as a residual pathway, preserving pretrained computation while learning complementary token-specific information in a scalable manner. On OLMo-2 1B, STAPLE improves over continued dense training by 4.27 points on HumanEval, 2.80 on MBPP, 2.27 on GSM8K, and 1.65 on DROP. Average performance increases with static capacity, and improvements persist on the larger OLMo-2 7B backbone. STAPLE also outperforms static sparse baselines such as STEM and an Engram-style model, and achieves a higher average score than an MoE upcycling baseline while decoding 2x faster with less than half its GPU model memory and measured GPU energy per token in our throughput-oriented decoding evaluation. Importantly, despite introducing billions of parameters late in training, our host-offloaded implementation keeps generation throughput within 1.5% and training throughput within 3% of the dense baseline, while caching only the ~5% most frequent embeddings on GPU. These results show that static sparse memory can provide a sample-efficient, scalable, and sustainable path for expanding pretrained models without sparse pretraining from scratch.
authors: Ranajoy Sadhukhan, Euijin Hong, Sheng Cao, Zechun Liu, Shuowei Jin, Sha Li, Changlong Yu, Xin Liu, Qin Lu, Zhenyu Shi, Priyanka Nigam, Beidi Chen
bullets: Addresses the cost and data demands of pretraining sparse architectures, especially limitations of MoE upcycling.
Retains pretrained FFN up-projections and adds STEM-based token-indexed embeddings as complementary residual information.
Performance improves with static memory capacity and transfers to both 1B and 7B OLMo-2 backbones.
Outperforms dense continued training and static sparse baselines across coding, math, and question-answering benchmarks.
Compared with an MoE upcycling baseline, achieves higher average performance while decoding 2× faster and using less GPU memory; throughput stays close to dense training and generation baselines.
papers.selection_reason: Static sparse memory upcycling improves LLM capacity and inference efficiency.
papers.title: STAPLE: Static Sparse Upcycling of Pretrained Checkpoints via Embedding Modules
papers.tldr: STAPLE efficiently expands pretrained LLMs by adding token-indexed static sparse embeddings as a residual pathway, improving task performance with minimal training and decoding overhead.

papers.abstract: Agentic large language models now tackle complex tasks, yet strategic reasoning over long horizons is under-studied: most agentic benchmarks are short and episodic, and performance on long tasks is hard to dissect into stored knowledge, reasoning and luck. We introduce SpireBench, in which models play the complete commercial deck-builder Slay the Spire (StS), where early decisions decide long-term success. Across 20 large language models (LLMs) at the game's highest difficulty, frontier models beat heuristic baselines and match the average human player but remain far behind experts. This gap widens as the run lengthens: the strongest models win the first act as often as experts, then fall behind. What separates strong models from weak is how well they play each fight; all of them misjudge risk over a run, preserving health rather than spending it to grow stronger. A comprehensive, self-consistent renaming of every game term shows that part of their performance rests on prior knowledge of the game, and models do not improve from the memories they write across runs, which are often wrong and overly cautious. Our harness is the first to give a model the complete original game, and we compare it with existing harnesses. Overall, SpireBench offers an unsaturated long-horizon benchmark with tools to locate where and why agents fail.
authors: Scott C. Lowe, Sander W. Keemink
bullets: Tests 20 LLMs at Slay the Spire’s highest difficulty against heuristic baselines and human performance.
Models win the first act about as often as experts, but their performance declines as runs become longer.
Stronger models distinguish themselves mainly through better fight-by-fight play, while all models misjudge long-term risk.
Agents tend to preserve health instead of spending it to become stronger, and written memories across runs are often incorrect, overly cautious, and unhelpful.
Renaming game terms shows that performance partly depends on prior game knowledge; the benchmark is designed to diagnose long-horizon failure modes.
papers.selection_reason: Benchmark evaluating long-horizon agentic LLM play and memory written across runs; directly relevant to agent memory.
papers.title: SpireBench: Evaluating Long-Horizon Strategic Play of Agentic Models with Slay the Spire
papers.tldr: SpireBench evaluates long-horizon strategic reasoning by having LLM agents play the complete game Slay the Spire, revealing that frontier models match average humans early but remain well below experts over full runs.

papers.abstract: A latent recurrent language model applies a shared block of layers repeatedly, so one checkpoint can trade inference compute for accuracy by changing the loop count. At one loop, however, such models typically fall well short of a non-recurrent model of the same size, a one-loop tax that makes a separate non-recurrent model the better choice whenever latency matters. We present Elastic Latent Recurrence (ELR), a recipe for training looped language models without this tax. At one loop, an ELR model costs the same to serve as a non-recurrent model of the same size and, trained on the same data, reaches similar accuracy. Each additional loop then buys more accuracy for more inference compute. Three choices make this work: a gated state update with a learned step size, loop counts mixed within each optimizer update, and conditioning each pass on its loop index and budget. The first two preserve one-loop accuracy, and the third lowers loss at every additional loop. Mixed depths can be introduced late in pretraining to limit the added training cost, and with zero-initialized conditioning added at the switch, this late schedule reaches lower loss than mixed-depth training from scratch. In MoE models, reusing first-loop expert routes on later loops cuts mixed-depth update time by 11.7% with no measurable change in accuracy. At inference, keeping only the last loop's attention KV cache holds attention KV memory at its one-loop level while retaining most of the gain from additional loops. On 4B dense and 30B-A3B MoE hybrid models, ELR at one loop is 0.52 points below and 1.04 points above its matched baseline on a ten-task average, and four loops add 7.25 and 4.75 points. Carried through post-training, the recipe yields Koi-4B, a single checkpoint that scores an estimated 18 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at one loop, matching Qwen3.5-4B, and 29 at four loops.
